column4: The section's dictionary sense of هدي is made spatial here: sacrificial animals have a fixed term, then their mahill is at the Ancient House.
Until the hady reaches its mahill directly supplies the section's animal, journey, and appointed arrival.
Its expiation is a hady reaching the Ka'bah, explicitly joining the offering to the House it must attain.
The hady is held back from its mahill while pilgrims are barred from the Sacred Mosque: the section's homeward movement is deliberately interrupted.
The verse makes hady, garlanded animals, and people heading for the Sacred House jointly inviolable, matching the section's protected offering and traveler.
The Ka'bah, sacred months, hady, and garlands are made a support for people; it gathers the House, seasonal marker, offering, and public assembly.
Each community's rite includes remembering God's name over the cattle He provided, joining the section's an'am, sacrifice, and named worship.
The sacrificial camels are among God's ritual signs; His name is pronounced over them, and their meat is shared after sacrifice.
God subjects the animals so people magnify Him for having guided them, exactly joining the tamed animal, worship, and hidayah in the section.
Abraham is told to proclaim pilgrimage, and people come by every distant route, giving the section's movement toward the House its gathered, public scene.
Pilgrims witness benefits and remember God's name on provided cattle on known days; this extends the named-animal scene of 22:34 and 22:36.
After the cattle rites, pilgrims complete their rites and circumambulate the Ancient House; its own contribution is the arrival-act at the section's destination.
Honoring God's ritual signs is piety of the hearts, furnishing the inward meaning of the marked sacrificial animals in the following scene.
The first House is blessed and guidance for the worlds; House and huda stand together in a form especially close to the section's road ending at a home.
The House has clear signs, entrance into it is safety, and pilgrimage to it is a duty: destination, marker, sanctuary, and journey cohere.
God makes the House a place of return and security, making explicit the section's claim that the guided route has a home and safe arrival.
Abraham settles his offspring in the barren valley beside God's Sacred House, asking that hearts incline there and that they receive provision.
The command is to worship the Lord of this House, coupling the home itself to the section's عبادة strand.
The Lord of the House feeds people after hunger and secures them from fear, completing the section's provision and refuge motifs.
One who seeks protection is sheltered until hearing God's word and then delivered to his مأمن; it is the section's asylum-seeker brought to safety.
The queen sends a هدية to Solomon, the Qur'an's direct instance of the section's secondary h-d-y sense of a gift carried to another.
Solomon rejects the gift and turns its value back on its senders, reversing the section's friendly gift that reaches its proper recipient.
The command to eat what God's name was mentioned over directly realizes the section's named animal at the meal.
For trained hunting animals, God's name is mentioned over what they catch; the named-animal rule is extended beyond the Hajj offering.
It asks why believers should not eat that over which God's name has been mentioned, clarifying the positive command in 6:118.
In houses God has permitted to be raised, His name is remembered and He is glorified; it gives a House, elevated mention, and worship parallel.
God sets landmarks and stars by which travelers are guided. The section explicitly links its wasam/ma'lam observation to marks that orient a route.
God calls to the Abode of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, making the path-to-home relation explicit.
The verse calls this the straight path of the Lord; the next ayah supplies its safe dwelling, so this row establishes the route itself.
Those who heed the path have an Abode of Peace with their Lord, who is their protector; 6:126 supplies the straight-path neighbor.
Those following God's good pleasure are guided to paths of peace and brought from darkness into light, a plural-path form of the section's safe arrival.
After the descent, whoever follows God's guidance has neither fear nor grief, casting guidance as the protection needed after leaving an earlier dwelling.
After humanity's descent, divine guidance is promised; following it prevents both going astray and misery, a direct boundary for the homeward path.
People admitted to the Garden say God guided them to this; the utterance names a completed destination rather than guidance as abstraction.
Faith guides believers toward gardens beneath which rivers run, pairing hidayah with an inhabited final place.
God will guide the slain in His way and set their condition right; the following ayah gives the destination this guidance opens.
God admits them to the Garden He has made known to them; this row supplies the recognized dwelling reached after the guidance of 47:5.
Moses describes the Lord as giving every thing its created form and then guiding it, matching the section's interest in what is made fit and led.
The Creator proportioned, determined, and then guided, a compressed account of fitting and directing that illuminates the section's tamed, destined creature.
God guides travelers through the darknesses of land and sea, a literal navigation scene for the section's road-and-arrival sense of h-d-y.
As Moses turns toward Midian, he asks that his Lord guide him to the sound way; this is a traveler seeking a real destination.
Noah asks, "My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing-place"; it is a direct prayer to be brought safely into a dwelling after travel.
Worship Me; this is a straight path directly binds the section's عبادة strand to the path it asks to be shown.
Upon mounting what God has subjected, travelers remember His favor and declare His transcendence; the verse makes riding a tamed creature an act of praise.
After the mount-and-praise of 43:13, the travelers confess that they will return to their Lord, adding the ultimate homeward horizon.
The ayah places the making of spouses from one soul beside the eight pairs of cattle, a rare Qur'anic meeting of the section's bride and herd branches.
God makes spouses from people and pairs from cattle, again holding marriage and herd together in one generative scene.
Marriage is described as a solemn covenant, giving Qur'anic form to the section's bride being joined to a husband and the protecting word of covenant.
Women are to receive their bridal gifts graciously; the gift branch is placed inside the bride-and-marriage branch rather than mere exchange.
God says that He married Zaynab to Muhammad, a direct Qur'anic instance of a woman being joined to her husband by a decisive act.
Spouses are made so that people find tranquility in them, giving the section's bride brought home an inward form of settled belonging.
Those already settled in the home and faith love the emigrants and make room for them, a communal counterpart to the protected person received by a people.
Those who gave the emigrants shelter and help are bound by mutual responsibility, while a treaty limits intervention; refuge and covenant occur together.
Treaties with partners who have not violated them are to be honored to their term, supplying the reliable word that the section says protects a seeker.
The treaty made near the Sacred Mosque is to be upheld while the other party upholds it, tying covenantal protection to the House's precinct.
Abraham asks that the city be made secure, grounding the section's inviolable House and safe destination in a prayer for sanctuary.
Abraham asks that this be a secure city and that its people receive fruits, combining safe settlement and provision near the House.
The objection to following guidance is answered with God's secure sanctuary, to which fruits are brought; huda, refuge, and provision are explicit together.
God has made a secure sanctuary while people around it are snatched away, sharpening the House as a protected place.
The believers will enter the Sacred Mosque in security and without fear, resolving the interruption of hady and pilgrimage in 48:25.
Prayer and sacrifice alike belong wholly to God; it makes the offering's purpose the nearness and devotion emphasized in the section.
The command to pray to the Lord and sacrifice binds sacrificial action directly to worship.
Safa and Marwa are God's ritual signs, and their circuit belongs to Hajj or umrah; they broaden the section's marked pilgrimage landscape.
Hajj has known months, giving Qur'anic substance to the section's season as a marked time of gathering.
At the Hajj stations people remember God as He guided them after earlier error; rite, gathered place, remembrance, and hidayah converge.
Pilgrims are told to depart from where the people depart and ask forgiveness; its own contribution is the shared movement of the Hajj assembly.
Numbered days of remembrance close the Hajj instructions; this row contributes the calendared, communal finish to the pilgrimage scene.
Abraham and Ishmael ask to be shown their rites while raising the House's foundations; it supplies the rite-request surrounding the House of 2:125.
In the qiblah dispute, God guides whom He wills to a straight path; orientation toward the House becomes a test of being directed.
The Prophet is commanded to turn his face toward the Sacred Mosque, a concrete bodily direction toward the section's House.
Wherever travelers emerge from, they are to turn toward the Sacred Mosque; this makes the House a direction carried through movement.
The repeated qiblah command ends with completion of God's favor and the hope that people will be guided, linking direction, نعمة, and hidayah.
The Sacred Mosque is for resident and visitor alike, while intending violation there brings warning; it frames the House as a guarded shared destination.
A public proclamation is made on the day of the greater pilgrimage, giving the section's Hajj gathering its covenantal public setting.
After their appointed year, polytheists are barred from the Sacred Mosque; this is a boundary around the protected House and its pilgrimage space.
Fulfill contracts immediately precedes the prohibition on violating hady and House-bound pilgrims in 5:2; this row supplies the covenant principle.
Meat dedicated to other than God and slaughter on idolatrous altars are forbidden, marking the boundary around the section's God-named offering.
Land game is forbidden while in consecrated pilgrimage even as sea game is allowed, distinguishing Hajj restraint from ordinary animal use.
God has not instituted the pagan animal designations bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah, and ham; fabricated consecrations contrast with His appointed hady.
Do not eat what God's name has not been mentioned over; it states the negative boundary of the named-animal practice in 6:118.
People assign shares of crops and cattle to God and to partners, then manipulate them; this corrupts the offering's Godward purpose.
Invented livestock prohibitions include animals over which God's name is not pronounced, a direct reversal of the section's named sacrifice.
Meat dedicated to other than God is prohibited, distinguishing true invocation over food or offering from rival dedication.
The dietary prohibition includes what was dedicated to other than God, repeating the naming boundary in a legal list.
The same exclusion of what was dedicated to other than God places the named-animal rule within God's provision and necessity allowance.
The two sons of Adam each bring a qurban, and acceptance depends on God-consciousness; sacrifice is shown as an approach whose meaning exceeds the object.
Abraham's vision of sacrificing his son makes surrender and obedience the inner test behind a sacrificial scene.
The son is ransomed with a great sacrifice, making deliverance and offering meet.
God's she-camel is a sign and must not be harmed; its protected status parallels the inviolable animal in the House-bound offering scene.
Thamud hamstrings the she-camel after the prohibition, a reversal of the care owed to a divinely protected animal.
The she-camel is God's sign and is to graze unharmed; the repeated scene reinforces animal inviolability outside the Hajj rite.
After killing the she-camel, Thamud are given only three days; violating the protected sign has the opposite outcome to honoring God's symbols.
The she-camel has an allotted drinking turn beside the people's turn, presenting an animal with a protected, regulated claim.
The sending of the she-camel is a test, making this exceptional animal a divinely charged sign rather than mere livestock.
Water is divided between the people and the she-camel; the verse gives the animal a publicly observed right within the community.
The messenger warns about God's she-camel and its watering, keeping the animal's protected status at the center of the warning.
They deny and hamstring the she-camel, so the town is leveled; it is the destructive opposite of honoring a protected animal.
Among cattle are animals for carrying burdens and for food; this supplies the serviceable herd beneath the section's sacrificial camel.
Cattle provide warmth, benefits, and food, making the herd a received provision before it becomes an offering.
The animals carry burdens to a land people could scarcely reach themselves, a travel-and-arrival role close to the section's carried homeward animal.
From cattle skins God makes houses and portable shelters, an unusual direct meeting of herd, travel, and home.
God creates cattle for people and makes them theirs; the following ayat specify the tractable service central to the section's tamed animal.
God makes cattle tractable, so some are mounts and some are eaten; this is a close Qur'anic parallel to the section's uysallaştırılmış camel.
Cattle provide benefits and drinks, completing the provision side of the herd that is later offered and shared.
God creates cattle so that people may ride some and eat some, repeating the controlled animal's double use as mount and food.
Cattle carry people's needs and their riders alongside ships, making them vehicles toward human purposes and destinations.
God makes ships and cattle for riding, preparing the concrete mount-and-journey scene developed in 43:13.
God makes spouses, children, and good provision; it connects the bride branch to household formation and sustenance.
The unmarried are to be married, and God may enrich them from His bounty; marriage is treated as a gathered household rather than private possession.
Divorced women are not to be prevented from marrying their husbands again when they agree honorably, a concrete reopening of the marital home.
A mate is made from the one soul so that he may find tranquility with her, giving the bride branch a form of settled attachment.
The father of Midian offers one daughter in marriage to Moses on a term of service, a narrated act of joining a bride to a husband.
Moses accepts the marriage term and asks God to witness it; this row supplies the binding completion of the proposal in 28:27.
A husband who has given his wife even a great amount may not take it back, guarding the bridal gift after it has been given.
The queen's fear that kings ruin towns explains why the gift of 27:35 is diplomatic rather than the section's gift to a beloved friend.
Solomon orders the envoy to return; after 27:36 refuses the gift, this row turns the intended approach into an opposed return.
The emigrants have been driven from their homes and possessions while seeking God's favor; it supplies the vulnerability answered by 59:9's welcome.
The emigrants and those who sheltered and helped them are affirmed together; it confirms the refuge relationship detailed in 8:72.
People attached to a group with whom there is a treaty are exempt from attack when they withdraw from fighting, a legal shelter created by covenant.
Those who emigrate after being wronged are promised a good settlement in this world, a divine answer to departure from home.
Those who emigrate and are killed or die will receive good provision and be admitted by an entrance they approve, joining provision to a welcomed arrival.
God promises to establish believers in the land and exchange their fear for security, the social scale of the section's safe place.
The companions are told to take refuge in the cave, where their Lord will spread mercy and prepare their affair; physical shelter becomes divinely given safety.
Noah's son seeks a mountain to protect him from the flood, but Noah says none protects from God's command except those granted mercy; a false safe place fails.
If hypocrites could find a refuge, cave, or place of entry, they would rush toward it; flight into shelter is contrasted with the honored asylum of 9:6.
The three who lagged behind learn that there is no refuge from God except with Him, relocating all secure arrival to the divine side.
No one can alter God's words, and none can find a refuge apart from Him; this supplies the ultimate limit on human protection.
God protects while none can be protected against Him, making the efficacy of every asylum depend on the true Protector.
Humans seeking refuge with jinn only increase their burden; it is a contrary version of seeking protection from a people.
The messenger says none can protect him from God and he will find no refuge besides Him, setting the boundary for every shelter.
Those who trusted their fortresses to protect them from God are reached from where they did not expect; fortified dwelling is not guaranteed sanctuary.
The prayer asks for a truthful entrance and a truthful exit with supporting authority, a compact invocation for rightly conducted departure and arrival.
Those who believe have goodness and a beautiful homecoming; in the surrounding guidance passage, the end of turning to God is named as return.
Pharaoh's wife asks for a house near God in Paradise and rescue from oppression, joining desired dwelling and refuge in one prayer.
Those who obey God and the Messenger are with the people upon whom God has bestowed favor; it expands the Fatiha's أنعمت into a gathered destination-community.
God says He would guide the obedient to a straight path, retaining the request's path language as a destination-directed divine act.
After God has guided us, should we be turned back like one lured bewildered while companions call him toward guidance? It dramatizes loss and recall of a route.
The Prophet says his Lord has guided him to a straight path, an upright religion of Abraham; guidance is inseparable from a lived way of worship.
The question contrasts one who guides to truth with one needing guidance, clarifying the guide-led relation behind ihdina.
Every people has a guide, giving the section's request for guidance a human-prophetic counterpart.
The Book brings people from darkness to light by their Lord's permission, toward the path of the Mighty and Praiseworthy.
The messengers say God has guided them to their ways; their trust turns received guidance into a route they can inhabit.
Mountains, rivers, and roads are set in the earth so people may be guided; 16:16 then identifies landmarks and stars for that movement.
The Qur'an guides to what is most upright, making the section's requested route a scriptural direction rather than a bare line.
The cave's opening is described in a protected physical scene, and the verse declares that the one God guides is truly guided; refuge and hidayah overlap.
Abraham asks his father to follow him so he can guide him to an even path, a personal guide inviting another into a sound route.
The ending asks who are the companions of the even path and who has been guided, making right arrival a disclosed distinction.
Believers' hearts become humble before the revealed truth, and God guides them to a straight path; worshipful receptivity is its route.
At the sea Moses says his Lord is with him and will guide him; guidance appears at a threatened crossing toward safety.
Abraham names God as the One who created him and then guides him, pairing originating creation with ongoing direction.
The Prophet cannot guide whom he loves, while God guides whom He wills; it identifies the divine agent addressed by ihdina.
Those who strive for God are guided to His ways, retaining the image of plural routes that lead toward the One sought.
God's covenant with Adam's children forbids worship of Satan; this supplies the covenantal boundary for the straight worship-path in 36:61.
Satan has led many astray after the command to worship God on the straight path, the route's active contrary pull.
The condemned are told to be led to the path of Hell, a severe reversal in which guidance-language carries people to the wrong final abode.
Moses and Aaron are guided to the straight path, a prophetic recurrence of the route requested in the section.
Thamud are shown guidance but prefer blindness over it, a stated refusal of the path's offered direction.
The believing man tells his people to follow him and he will guide them to the way of rectitude, echoing the guide-to-path relation.
The revealed spirit is made a light through which God guides whom He wills to a straight path, linking the path to heard divine speech.
God spreads out the earth and makes paths in it so people may be guided, a literal terrain-and-route counterpart to the section's way home.
Jesus says to worship God, his Lord and theirs; this is a straight path, repeating the worship-and-route conjunction.
The jinn say the revealed Book guides to truth and to a straight path, making heard scripture a guide for travelers.
In the Hudaibiyah passage God promises to guide the Prophet to a straight path; 48:25 and 48:27 give that promise a House-and-pilgrimage setting.
Guidance to faith is named as God's favor, directly illuminating the section's lexical meeting of an'amta and ihdina.
The jinn call the Qur'an a recitation that guides to right conduct, a listener's response close to the protected seeker hearing God's word in 9:6.
God has shown the human the way, whether grateful or ungrateful; the verse makes the path a responsible response to provision.
God shows the two elevated ways, presenting a visible choice of routes rather than an undifferentiated journey.
God declares that guidance rests with Him, reinforcing why the section's request is addressed to God.
God found the Prophet searching and guided him, a speaker-centered memory of being brought from lack of direction.
God assigns Abraham the place of the House and tells him to cleanse it for those who circle, stand, bow, and prostrate; this gives the destination its worshipful origin.
Honoring God's sanctities is joined here to the lawfulness of livestock except stated restrictions; it extends the House passage's sacred boundary around the section's herd.
Abraham and Ishmael raise the House's foundations and ask acceptance; this row supplies the constructed home immediately before their request to be shown the rites.
God tests pilgrims with game within reach of hands and spears; its own contribution is the animal-restraint test for which 5:95 then gives hady expiation.
Giving water to pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque are named as House-related services, giving the gathering a human custodial scene.
When believers were few and feared being snatched away, God gave them shelter, aid, and good provision; asylum, safety, and provision are explicit together.
One who emigrates for God finds many places of refuge and abundance, and even departure from home cut short by death remains a completed Godward journey.
Believing women arrive as emigrants, are not returned to unbelievers, and may enter new marriages after bridal payments; asylum, bride, and gift meet in one legal scene.
Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak. The section's asylum-seeker and its Rabb branch meet in a direct formula of refuge.
Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of people, another direct rendering of the protected seeker turning to a Rabb.
The protector invoked in 114:1 is named King of people, bringing the Malik root's sovereign sense into the refuge formula.
We raised your remembrance is the direct Qur'anic counterpart to the section's s-m-w claim that a name raises the mention of the one named.
We shall brand him on the snout uses the section's w-s-m stamp branch as a punitive mark, reversing the communal marker of the pilgrimage season.
The believers' visible mark is on their faces from prostration; in the same Hudaibiyah-House setting, worship itself yields a recognisable sign.
God places linked towns on a measured route and commands travel through them safely by night and day, a concrete scene of protected movement between dwellings.
They ask for their journey-stages to be lengthened and wrong themselves, after which they are dispersed; it reverses the safe, measured route of 34:18.
A town once safe, tranquil, and supplied from every place tastes hunger and fear after ingratitude, the contrary outcome to the House's provision and security.
Those whose faith is not mixed with wrongdoing have security and are rightly guided, directly pairing the section's safe arrival with hidayah.
God guides to Himself whoever turns back to Him, giving guidance an explicitly Godward destination.
The cave youths believe in their Lord and are increased in guidance; this supplies the inner hidayah of the refuge scene continued in 18:16-17.
In the Hudaibiyah passage, God sends His Messenger with guidance and true religion; it gives the surrounding House-and-pilgrimage episode its guiding mission.
The ayah compares one moving face-down with one walking upright on a straight path, a bodily reversal that makes guided travel perceptible.
The livestock polemic explicitly names the camel pair and cattle pair, making the section's an'am-camel identification concrete within Qur'anic animal law.
This is an object-level parallel: the section identifies the hady's animal as a camel, while this ayah calls for reflection on how the camel was created rather than on sacrifice.
A lexical bridge with a real limit: the section's m-l-k marriage sense meets the ayah's ownership sense, which it distinguishes from marriage sought with wealth and chastity.
The verse permits marriage to believing women in an ownership context with their people's permission and bridal payments, bringing m-l-k, marriage, covenantal consent, and gift together.
Remember God's favor and the covenant He bound with the believers joins the section's an'amta favor branch to its Rabb/covenant branch.
Those who bar access to the Sacred Mosque are denied true guardianship of it; the verse clarifies that protection of the House belongs with the reverent, not obstructers.
